For a circular orbit the geometric probability that a planet transits is, to first order,  

 P(transit) ≈ R★ / a ,

where R★ is the stellar radius and a the orbital semi-major axis.  
Because the two host stars have the same radius, the ratio of the two transit probabilities is simply

 P₁ / P₂ = a₂ / a₁ .

Using Kepler’s third law (a ∝ M★^1/3 P^2/3) we find

 a₁ / a₂ = (M₁^1/3 P₁^2/3) / (M₂^1/3 P₂^2/3).

Given  
• P₁ = P₂ / 3  (Planet 1’s period is three times shorter)  
• M₁ = 2 M₂   (Planet 1’s star is twice as massive)  

Insert these:

 a₁ / a₂ = (2 M₂)^1/3 (P₂/3)^2/3 / (M₂^1/3 P₂^2/3)  
     = 2^{1/3} / 3^{2/3} ≈ 1.2599 / 2.0801 ≈ 0.605 .

Therefore

 P₁ / P₂ = a₂ / a₁ ≈ 1 / 0.605 ≈ 1.65 .

Planet 1 thus has about 1.65 times (≈65 %) greater chance to transit than Planet 2, so Planet 1 is the better target.
